meta.scope: Manual static review of the `backend/` application in the eazyreminder monorepo at branch `feature/ongoing-work` (commit cf9f46b). Covers the HTTP entry point and Apache rewrite rules, the global and route middleware chain, all 60 API routes and their 14 controllers, the 20 Blade admin routes, the unrouted AdminApi controllers, the five service classes, the authentication, social-login, QR-web-login and subscription-entitlement paths, all 67 migrations, the scheduler and cron dispatch path, and the shipped configuration templates. The sibling `mobile/` Flutter application in the same repository was NOT reviewed and is out of scope for this report. A previously reviewed deployed snapshot of an older revision of this backend is cited only where it establishes a runtime fact the source alone cannot (the document-root layout and the use of a cached config); every finding is otherwise evidenced in the current source. No automated SAST, dependency-vulnerability scan, or dynamic testing was performed.

verdict.summary: Production release is blocked. Two independent authentication bypasses let an attacker who holds any valid Firebase ID token — obtainable free, for a phone number they own — take over an arbitrary account: one by naming a victim's email on `/login`, the other by binding their own Firebase UID permanently to a victim's account on `/social-login`. Alongside these sit an unauthenticated entitlement webhook, a cross-tenant delete, a cross-tenant share, an unrestricted upload, an unauthenticated job endpoint that leaks other users' reminder titles, a hardcoded QA phone allowlist that grants paid features, and a deployment layout that serves the application root to the internet. The codebase is nonetheless improving: everything written in the last few months — the share, todo, QR-login, referral and app-config code — gets identity, authorisation and error logging right. The defects are concentrated in the older controllers, and in every case a correct implementation of the same control already exists elsewhere in the repository to copy from.

blockers.text: Remove the passwordless email branch from `/api/login`; it mints a session token for any account given only its email address, and the middleware no longer constrains it.
Stop `/api/social-login` resolving accounts by an unverified request-body email, and never bind a Firebase UID to an account the token did not prove ownership of.
Apply the existing `admin.api` middleware (or an equivalent `is_admin` gate) to the Blade `/admin` route group.
Authenticate the RevenueCat webhook from cached config with a fail-closed check, exactly as `AppConfigController::update` already does.
Scope `DELETE /api/user-delete/{id}` to the authenticated user, and make `shareFolder` derive `sender_id` from the session as `ShareController::createInvite` already does.
Reject attacker-chosen upload filenames and directories, and validate file type on every upload path rather than only when `is_app` is truthy.
Authenticate `GET /api/cron-reminders` or move it to the scheduler, and delete the `echo` that leaks other users' reminder titles.
Move the Laravel application root out of the web document root and rotate every credential that has been reachable there.

objective.narrative: To establish the security, architectural and operational state of the EazyReminder backend as it stands in source on the active development branch, and to convert what was found into a prioritised, costed remediation plan. This review supersedes an earlier assessment that was performed against a deployed filesystem snapshot; that snapshot has since been overtaken by roughly 6,000 lines of new application code, four new feature areas and eighteen new migrations. Findings are stated only where the path from an HTTP entry point to the concrete failure was traced end to end in the current source.

executiveSummary:
The EazyReminder backend is a Laravel 9 API serving a Flutter application that stores users' phone numbers, email addresses, reminder content, shared to-do boards and uploaded photographs, and that gates paid features on subscription state. Since the previous review the codebase has grown by about two thirds — QR web login, Google and Apple sign-in, referrals, share groups and invites, and a full to-do subsystem have all landed. That new work is the good news in this report, and it is genuinely good: it derives identity from the session, checks ownership before acting, indexes its tables, logs its exceptions, and guards its one administrative endpoint with a fail-closed constant-time comparison. The team knows how to build this correctly.

The bad news is that almost none of that discipline has been applied backwards, and the authentication layer has quietly become weaker rather than stronger. Two separate paths now hand an attacker somebody else's account. `/api/login` still carries a branch that looks a user up by email address and issues a session token without ever checking a password — and a middleware change made to accommodate social login removed the one constraint that used to make that branch awkward to reach, so it is now a single request away. `/api/social-login` will resolve an account from an email address supplied in the request body when the Firebase token carries no email claim, and if that account has no Firebase UID yet — which is true of every user who signed up by email OTP — it permanently binds the attacker's UID to it. Both were traced end to end; neither requires anything more than a free account of the attacker's own.

Around them sit six further confirmed defects of the same family: account deletion and folder sharing act on identifiers taken from the request body rather than the session, the RevenueCat webhook's shared-secret check is disabled by the cached configuration the deployment actually uses, file uploads let the client choose both the directory and the filename with type validation skipped entirely on one path, and the reminder-dispatch job is a public GET that mutates state and echoes other users' reminder titles into its response. A hardcoded allowlist grants full paid entitlement to two fixed phone numbers with no environment guard. The deployment compounds all of it by serving the Laravel application root as the web document root, where the only protected file is the one literally named `.env`.

What makes this tractable is that every one of those defects has a correct sibling in the same repository. `ShareController` validates the sender against the session; `AppConfigController` reads its secret from config and fails closed; `TodoController` refuses to act without a session user; the new migrations index their foreign keys; `admin.api` middleware exists and does exactly the `is_admin` check the Blade panel lacks. The remediation is largely a matter of propagating patterns the team has already written, not inventing them. The recommended programme is 108.5 man-days across three phases; Phase 1 closes every production blocker in 35 days and requires no structural change.

scorecard.narrative: Every dimension is scored on the codebase as a whole, which means the newer subsystems pull the numbers up and the older ones pull them down. Security stays at the floor because two confirmed account-takeover paths and a hardcoded entitlement backdoor outweigh the good work elsewhere, and because no automated control exists that would have caught any of them. Data and architecture have moved up half a point each on the strength of the new migrations and the emerging service layer. DevOps is unchanged at the floor: still no pipeline, no environment separation and no infrastructure definition anywhere in the repository.

dimensions.label: Code Maintainability

dimensions.label: DevOps Maturity
dimensions.keyGap: No CI pipeline of any kind in the repository (G1), no IaC (G2), no staging environment (G9), no rollback path. The repo ships the forwarding `index.php` and root `.htaccess` that make the application root the document root (F12).

dimensions.label: Data Integrity & DB Health
dimensions.keyGap: The eight newest tables are properly indexed and keyed, but the six core legacy tables — reminders, folders, users, notifications, reminder_files, share_folder_requests — still carry no index or foreign key at all (F17). A login from a new device irreversibly deletes the user's reminders and files outside a transaction (F11).

systemModel.purpose: A reminder and light task-management backend. Users register with a phone number verified by Firebase phone OTP, an email address verified by a backend-issued email OTP, or a Google/Apple identity via Firebase. They create reminders carrying a title, description, schedule and optionally an uploaded photograph, document or audio note; organise them into folders; maintain shared to-do boards with invited collaborators; share folders, reminders and boards with other users by phone or email; earn referral credit; sign in to a browser by scanning a QR code from the phone app; and receive push notifications through Firebase Cloud Messaging when a reminder falls due. Paid tiers, sold through the app stores and reconciled by RevenueCat webhooks, raise the storage quota and unlock sharing. The data held is personal and identifying: phone numbers, email addresses, device identifiers, free-text reminder and task content, collaborator relationships, and user-uploaded images and documents.
systemModel.actors: Anonymous internet callers reach six routes with no credential: `cron-reminders`, `insert-subscription`, `check-reminder-available`, `revenuecat-webhook`, and the two QR web-login endpoints. Callers presenting the static header `os_key: PRP-ANDROID` reach registration, login, social login, email OTP and app-config. Authenticated app users hold a JWT and reach the 45 routes behind `jwt.verify`. Administrators reach the Blade panel at `/admin`. Firebase and RevenueCat are external systems whose assertions the backend consumes. The realistic attacker is a registered app user: registration is free, requires only a phone number the attacker controls, and immediately yields a JWT plus a valid Firebase ID token — which is precisely the credential set both account-takeover paths, the cross-tenant share and the cross-tenant delete require.
systemModel.dataFlows: Request → Apache (root `.htaccess`: serves any file that exists on disk, otherwise rewrites to `index.php`) → `backend/index.php` → `public/index.php` → Laravel kernel → global middleware (TrustProxies, HandleCors, ValidatePostSize, TrimStrings) → `api` group (`throttle:api`, SubstituteBindings) → `auth.appUser` (static `os_key` header check) → `throttle:auth` or `throttle:web-login` → `verify.firebase` on register/login/social-login/update-token/verify-phone → `jwt.verify` on the authenticated group → controller → service (on newer paths) or Eloquent directly (on older ones) → MySQL. Uploads land on the `public` disk and are served back through the `public/storage` symlink, i.e. from inside the document root. Authentication has three entry paths: phone (Firebase ID token whose `phone_number` claim is cross-checked against the body, but only when the body carries a phone), email (backend OTP, hashed, five attempts, ten-minute TTL), and social (Firebase ID token, resolved by UID then by email). QR web login is a fourth: the browser creates a 48-character token, the phone confirms it under its JWT, and the browser polls once to collect a one-time session handoff. Reminder dispatch runs on a separate path: an external caller performs `GET /api/cron-reminders` every minute, which selects due reminders, advances their recurrence state and posts to FCM inline.

invariants.statement: A session token is only ever issued to a caller who has proved control of the account's verified phone number, email address or federated identity.
invariants.note: Violated twice and independently: the email+password branch of `login()` (F1) and the body-email fallback in `socialLogin()` (F2). No `Hash::check` is performed against any app user's password anywhere in the codebase.

invariants.statement: A Firebase UID is only ever attached to an account whose ownership the token proved.
invariants.note: `socialLogin()` writes the caller's UID onto any account matched by an unverified request-body email address that has no UID yet — a permanent, self-service binding.

invariants.statement: Administrative functions are reachable only by users flagged `is_admin = 1`.
invariants.note: The Blade `/admin` group is gated on `auth` alone. The `admin.api` middleware that performs exactly this check is registered in the kernel and applied to nothing.

invariants.statement: An authenticated session can only read, modify or delete rows belonging to its own user.
invariants.note: Also violated by F6 (share `sender_id`) and F7 (upload directory), and partially by F29. Upheld correctly in ShareController, TodoController and SyncController.

invariants.statement: Paid entitlement is only granted on an assertion the backend can verify came from the payment provider.
invariants.note: The webhook's guard reads `env()` under a cached config and never fires. A hardcoded phone allowlist (F9) grants the same entitlement, and the Apple receipt path (F21) discards its verification result.

invariants.statement: No secret, key or credential is retrievable over HTTP.
invariants.note: The repository is clean of secrets — verified — but it ships the front controller and `.htaccess` that make the application root the document root, and the deployed instance served the Firebase service-account keys and every `.env` backup from it.

invariants.statement: A file written by an upload cannot be chosen by the uploader to land outside their own storage area or under a name the web server will execute.
invariants.note: Both the directory and the filename remain attacker-controlled, and the type check is skipped entirely when `is_app=0`.

invariants.statement: A user's reminders and uploaded files are only deleted on that user's explicit instruction.
invariants.note: A free user logging in from a device other than the registration device still has all reminders, files and notifications deleted silently, outside a transaction.

invariants.statement: A session can be revoked before its token expires.
invariants.note: The `session_token` comparison was removed from `JwtMiddleware` to stop multi-device logouts, and nothing replaced it. With a 30-day TTL and no blacklist call anywhere, a leaked token cannot be retired.

invariants.statement: No request path reaches SQL with an unbound user-controlled value.
invariants.note: All raw-SQL sites interpolate server-side constants only — a literal extensions array and column names. Every user value reaches the query as a bound parameter. See refuted candidate 1.

invariants.statement: A failure in an external dependency fails closed rather than open.
invariants.note: The RevenueCat webhook fails open on a missing secret. `AppConfigController::update`, written later, fails closed on exactly the same shape of check — the correct pattern already exists in the codebase.

invariants.statement: Every failure is recorded somewhere an engineer can find it.
invariants.note: 50 of 81 catch blocks discard the exception. The split is by vintage: ShareController logs 9 of 9 and TodoController 8 of 9, while ReminderController logs 5 of 22 and UserController 1 of 8.

invariants.statement: A single failing external call cannot prevent other users' reminders from being delivered.
invariants.note: `die()` inside the dispatch loop aborts the whole batch on the first cURL error, and the recurrence pointer of already-processed rows has moved, so they are not retried.

invariants.statement: Traffic to third-party APIs carrying a bearer token is protected by a verified TLS certificate.
invariants.note: `CURLOPT_SSL_VERIFYPEER = false` at five outbound FCM call sites — and the newest of them is in `FcmShareNotifier`, a service written during this development cycle, so the pattern is still spreading.

invariants.statement: Every application table enforces referential integrity and is indexed for its access pattern.
invariants.note: True of the eight newest tables, false of the six core legacy ones. The practice changed without the existing schema being backfilled.

invariants.statement: Every change to production is reproducible from version control.
invariants.note: Improved: the repository is a real git repo with `composer.lock` tracked. But there is no CI, no environment separation and no deployment definition (see the missing capabilities), so what actually reaches the server is still unverifiable from the repository alone.

threatModel: The attacker to design against is a registered app user, because registration is free and yields the only credential the serious paths need: a valid Firebase ID token for an identity the attacker controls. From that position F1 gives them any account whose email address they know, and F2 gives them any email-registered account — permanently, by binding their own Firebase UID to it. F5 lets them destroy any account outright, F6 lets them extract a Pro user's folders and reminders into their own account, and F3 escalates them to administrator through the stock password-reset form. A weaker, entirely anonymous attacker still reaches F4 (grant paid entitlement to any user ID), F8 (drive reminder dispatch and read other users' reminder titles out of the response) and F12 (retrieve whatever the document root exposes on the deployed host). F9 sits slightly apart: anyone able to complete Firebase phone verification for one of two hardcoded numbers receives full paid entitlement, which is a business-revenue exposure rather than a data one. The paths compose badly — F4 grants the Pro status that F6 requires of its recipient, and F12 yields the Firebase service-account key that signs push notifications to every installed client.

coverage.method: Manual static review, single pass, read in execution order (Apache rewrite rules → `index.php` → HTTP kernel → middleware chain → route file → controller → service → model → migration). No automated tooling of any kind was run: no SAST, no dependency-vulnerability scanner, no linter, and no dynamic or runtime testing. Every candidate was confirmed by tracing it from a named HTTP entry point through the middleware that guards it to its concrete effect. Sibling comparison was used heavily and productively: this codebase contains correct and incorrect implementations of the same control side by side, and the correct one establishes that the other is a gap rather than a house style.

caveats: F9's reachability depends on whether the two hardcoded phone numbers are still configured as Firebase Console test numbers, which could not be verified from the repository. The allowlist itself is unconditional and present in production code regardless — that part is certain; only the ease of obtaining a token for those numbers is not.

F2 requires a Firebase ID token that carries no `email` claim. A phone-auth token satisfies this, and the relaxed middleware branch admits it, so the path is reachable — but whether the production Firebase project issues such tokens to the mobile clients in practice was not observable. The code accepts one regardless of who sends it.

F4 and F12 rest on two runtime facts established from a previously reviewed deployed snapshot of this backend: that `php artisan config:cache` is run on the host, and that the application root is the document root. Both are corroborated in the current source by the `env()` call and by the committed root `index.php` and `.htaccess`, but the deployed instance should be re-confirmed directly before the remediation order is fixed.

F7's most severe consequence — that an uploaded `.php` file would be executed by Apache from inside the document root — still depends on the host's PHP handler configuration, which was not observable. The finding is reported on what is certain: the filename and directory are attacker-controlled and type validation is absent on one path.

Multi-step write transactionality was sampled across the sync, share and todo paths rather than audited exhaustively; the todo subsystem in particular has a large sync surface that was read at the identity and authorisation level but not verified line by line for atomicity.

No runtime data was available, so all performance findings (F17, F24, F25, F26) are reasoned from query shape and schema rather than measured. Their estimates assume the legacy tables are in the tens of thousands of rows.

The Flutter client was not reviewed, so it is unknown whether it sends `is_app=0` (which removes upload validation in F7) or which of the login branches it actually calls. Neither uncertainty changes any finding: every branch is reachable by a hand-built request regardless of what the official client does.

findings.title: `/api/login` issues a session token for any account given only its email address, and the middleware change for social login removed the last constraint on it
findings.claim: The `email` + `password` branch of `login()` resolves the user by email address and mints a JWT without verifying the password, and `VerifyFirebaseIdToken` now waves through any request whose body omits `country_code`/`mobile` — so the branch is reachable with a Firebase token for any identity at all.

evidence.note: Branch selection. The validator on the following lines requires a password to be *present*, never that it be correct.

The user is resolved by email alone; `$data['password']` is never read again. A repository-wide sweep finds `Hash::check` only in the AdminApi controllers and the email-OTP service — never against an app user on this path.

The regression. Previously the middleware demanded a phone in the body and cross-checked it; now omitting the phone skips the check entirely, so a login request carrying only an email and a password passes straight through.
The only guards on the route are the rate limiter and the middleware above.

findings.reasoning: Violates the invariant that a session token is only issued to a caller who proved control of the account. The middleware proves something about the *token holder*; the controller then selects an account using a different, unproven field from the same body. That gap existed before, but the body previously had to carry a phone number that matched the token, which at least tied the request to a real identity the attacker owned. The relaxation added for social login removed even that, so the branch is now reachable by anyone holding any valid Firebase ID token.
findings.reproduction: Obtain any valid Firebase ID token (registering a throwaway phone account is sufficient). POST /api/login with header `os_key: PRP-ANDROID` and `X-Firebase-ID-Token: <token>`, body `{email: victim@example.com, password: 'anything'}` and no `mobile`/`country_code`. The middleware returns at the branch above, the controller takes the email+password path, and the response carries a JWT plus the victim's full user record.
findings.impact: Restores the integrity of the authentication boundary by ensuring a session is only ever issued to a caller who has proved control of the account, closing the most direct route to takeover of any account whose email address is known.
findings.refutation: Checked whether the relaxed middleware branch still constrains the request — it does not; it sets `firebase_phone` from whatever the token carries and calls `$next`. Checked whether the equality test later in the method helps: it compares `$user->email` against the submitted email, but the user was *found* by that email, so it is always true. Checked whether app users have password hashes that might make the branch behave: they do not, which makes it worse rather than better, since no correct password exists. Survives.
findings.remediation: Delete the `email` + `password` branch, and the `token`-only branch below it, outright — the product has no password authentication for app users. Reduce `login()` to exactly two paths: phone proven by a Firebase token whose claim matches, and email proven by a backend OTP. Then make the middleware assert positively what each route needs rather than skipping the check when a field is absent: `/login` and `/register` should require the phone claim, and only `/social-login`, `/verify-phone` and `/update-token` should take the phoneless path.

findings.title: `/api/social-login` binds the caller's Firebase UID to an account matched by an unverified request-body email, permanently taking it over
findings.claim: When the Firebase token carries no `email` claim, `socialLogin()` falls back to the email address in the request body, resolves an account by it, writes the caller's Firebase UID onto that account if it has none, and returns a JWT for it — a permanent takeover of every email-registered user.

evidence.note: The verified claim and the unverified body value are treated as interchangeable sources for the same variable.
The account is resolved by the unverified email and the attacker's UID is written onto it. From then on the attacker matches at line 570 by UID alone and no longer needs the email.
Email-OTP registration stores an empty `firebase_id` — so every account created that way satisfies the `empty($user->firebase_id)` precondition.
A JWT for the resolved account is minted and the full user record returned.
`firebase_email` is set only when the claim exists. A phone-auth token has no email claim, and the branch at line 94 admits such a token to this route because the body carries no phone.

findings.reasoning: The same structural error as F1 — proof about the caller and selection of the account come from different places — but with a worse outcome, because the binding is written to the database. After one request the attacker's Firebase identity *is* the victim's account: they can authenticate again at any time through the legitimate UID path, and the victim has no way to detect or undo it. It also survives any fix to F1.
findings.reproduction: Register a throwaway phone account and obtain its Firebase ID token, which carries `phone_number` but no `email`. POST /api/social-login with `os_key`, that token, and body `{provider: 'google', email: victim@example.com}` and no `mobile`/`country_code`. The middleware admits it, `firebase_email` is unset, the body email selects the victim, the attacker's UID is written to the victim's row, and a JWT for the victim is returned.
findings.impact: Guarantees a federated identity can only ever attach to an account that the identity provider actually vouched for, eliminating permanent account hijacking through the social sign-in path.
findings.refutation: Checked whether the middleware might reject a token with no email claim before it reaches the controller — it does not; the email claim is optional and the phone cross-check is skipped when the body has no phone. Checked whether the fallback is dead because Google and Apple tokens always carry an email — Apple with private-relay or a withheld email scope does not, and neither does a phone-auth token, which is the easier route in any case. Checked whether the UID write is guarded by an ownership test — it is guarded only by the target account *not already having* a UID, which is precisely the state of every email-OTP account. Survives.
findings.remediation: Use only `firebase_email` — the verified claim — when resolving or creating an account, and reject the request when the provider supplied no email rather than reading one from the body. Never write `firebase_id` onto an existing account inside a login path; account linking is a separate, explicitly authorised action performed by an already-authenticated user. Add a feature test asserting that a token with no email claim cannot select an account by a body-supplied address.

findings.title: The Blade admin panel has no role check, while the middleware that would enforce one sits registered and unused
findings.claim: The `/admin` route group is protected by Laravel's stock `auth` middleware with no role check, while `EnsureAdminApiUser` — which performs exactly the `is_admin` test required — is registered in the kernel as `admin.api` and applied to no route in this repository.

evidence.note: Wraps the dashboard, user list, user export, invoices, email settings and payment-gateway settings. No `can:`, no gate, no admin middleware.
Registration is disabled but password reset is not, so `/admin/password/reset` is live and resolves against the same unscoped `users` provider the mobile app registers into.
The correct check, already written.
Registered — and applied to nothing, because the AdminApi routes it was written for are not in this repository (F28).

findings.reasoning: Authentication has been substituted for authorisation. The design assumes only administrators can authenticate through the web guard, but app users occupy the same table and the stock reset broker lets them acquire a password they did not previously have. What makes this a clear gap rather than a design choice is that the team wrote the correct control during this same development cycle and simply never pointed it at the panel that is still live.
findings.reproduction: Register through the mobile app with an email address you control. Visit `/admin/password/reset`, request a link for that address and set a password. Log in at `/admin/login`; `auth` passes and `RouteServiceProvider::HOME` redirects to `/admin`, granting the full user list, the user export and the payment-gateway settings.
findings.impact: Restores least privilege on the administrative surface by requiring an explicit administrator role, preventing any end user from reaching the customer database, exports and payment configuration.
findings.refutation: Checked whether the Blade panel is dead code superseded by the AdminApi controllers — the opposite is true: the Blade routes are the ones registered and reachable, and the AdminApi controllers have no routes at all. Checked whether app users can authenticate at all given they are created without a password — the reset broker supplies one, and `config/auth.php` scopes it to no subset of users. Survives.
findings.remediation: Apply `admin.api` (or a `web`-guard equivalent) to the `/admin` group beside `auth` — a one-line change using the middleware that already exists. Then scope the web guard and the password broker to a provider filtered on `is_admin = 1`, so an app user cannot obtain a web password in the first place. Add a feature test asserting an authenticated non-admin receives 403 from `/admin`.

findings.title: The RevenueCat webhook is unauthenticated under the cached config, while the app-config endpoint beside it shows the correct pattern
findings.claim: The public webhook guards itself with `env('REVENUECAT_WEBHOOK_AUTH')` and skips the check when that value is empty; under `php artisan config:cache` — which the deployment runs — Laravel does not load `.env`, so `env()` returns null and every request is accepted.

evidence.note: Fail-open by construction: a missing secret disables the check instead of rejecting the request. `env()` outside a config file returns null once the config cache exists.
The correct sibling, written during this cycle: reads `config()` so it survives caching, fails closed on an empty key, and compares in constant time. This is the shape the webhook needs.
The effect: `is_paid`, `subscription_type`, `subscription_details` and `subscription_expiry_date` are all written from the request body for whatever `app_user_id` it names.
Outside every middleware group except `throttle:api` — no header check, no signature, no source-IP allow-list.

findings.reasoning: Two ordinary decisions combine into an open door: reading a secret with `env()` outside a config file, and writing the guard so that a missing secret disables it. The presence of the correct pattern a few files away makes this straightforwardly a gap rather than a considered trade-off. It also escalates — the paid status it grants is the precondition the recipient check in F6 requires.
findings.reproduction: POST /api/revenuecat-webhook with no Authorization header and body `{"event":{"type":"INITIAL_PURCHASE","app_user_id":"<any user id>","product_id":"premium"}}`. The named user is marked paid. Sending `{"type":"EXPIRATION"}` for another user's ID revokes their access.
findings.impact: Protects subscription revenue and restores trust in the entitlement record by ensuring only RevenueCat can change a user's paid status, and removes an unauthenticated write path into the users table.
findings.refutation: Checked whether the secret is simply unset, which would make this a configuration error rather than a code defect — it was present and 73 characters long in the deployed environment file, so the value exists and the runtime cannot see it. Confirmed from a deployed snapshot of this backend that `bootstrap/cache/config.php` is present and that `php artisan config:cache` appears in the host's shell history, and that a search of the cached config for `revenuecat` returns nothing, since the key is referenced from a controller rather than any file under `config/`. Survives.
findings.remediation: Move the secret into `config/services.php`, read it with `config()`, fail closed when it is empty, and compare with `hash_equals` — i.e. make this method structurally identical to `AppConfigController::update`. Add a boot-time or health-check assertion that production refuses to serve with the value unset.

findings.title: `DELETE /api/user-delete/{id}` deletes any user's account, reminders and files with no ownership check
findings.claim: The account-deletion handler resolves its target from the `{id}` path segment and never compares it to the authenticated user, so any user with a valid JWT can destroy any other account and all of its data.

evidence.note: `$id` comes straight from the route. `$this->user_id`, which the same controller uses correctly in `update()`, is never consulted.
The method then deletes the target's reminders and unlinks their files from disk, their folders, share requests, notifications and subscription history.
Inside the `jwt.verify` group, so authentication is required and authorisation is not performed.
Sibling comparison: every action in the newer TodoController opens by asserting a session user and scopes all work to it. `destroy()` is the anomaly.

findings.reasoning: Authentication mistaken for authorisation. The route is behind `jwt.verify`, which proves the caller is *a* user; nothing then checks they are *this* user. IDs are sequential integers, and the `firebase_id` alternative in the closure widens the match rather than narrowing it. The consequence is irreversible — files are unlinked from disk in the same pass.
findings.reproduction: As any registered user, DELETE /api/user-delete/2 with your own valid JWT and the `os_key` header. Account 2's reminders, uploaded files, folders, share requests and notifications are deleted and the account row removed or flagged deleted.
findings.impact: Prevents irreversible destruction of another customer's account and content by binding the deletion to the authenticated session, restoring tenant isolation across the API.
findings.refutation: Checked whether `jwt.verify` binds the route parameter to the token subject — it does not; it validates the token and checks `is_deleted`, nothing more. Checked for a policy or gate on the `User` model — none exists. Checked whether the `firebase_id` clause narrows the match to the caller — it broadens it, accepting either identifier. Survives.
findings.remediation: Delete the `{id}` parameter from the route and the method signature and operate on `authData()` alone — a user deleting their own account needs no identifier. If an administrative delete is required, put it behind the admin gate from F3. Add a feature test asserting a request naming another user's ID returns 403.

findings.title: Legacy folder sharing trusts a client-supplied `sender_id`, while the new share controller beside it validates the same field correctly
findings.claim: `ReminderController::shareFolder` takes the sharing user's identity from the request body and checks only that the *claimed* sender is entitled to share, never that they are the caller — so an attacker can forge a share request from any Pro user, address it to themselves, accept it, and receive that user's reminders and files.

evidence.note: The entitlement check is performed against the claimed sender, so naming a Pro victim satisfies it using the victim's own subscription. `$this->user_id` is never compared.
The folder-ownership check is likewise made against the claimed sender, so it passes on the victim's folders. For `share_type = 2` there is no ownership check at all.
The forged request is persisted with the victim as sender; acceptance then copies the victim's reminders and files to the receiver.
The correct sibling. `ShareController::createInvite` accepts the same field and rejects it when it does not match the session — proving the legacy handler is a gap, not house style.

findings.reasoning: Identity enters from the body and authorisation is decided against that same unverified value, which makes the check self-certifying. The new share subsystem accepts the identical field and validates it, so the two implementations disagree about who the sender is — and the older one is wrong.
findings.reproduction: As a user whose account can receive shares, POST /api/share-folder with `{sender_id: <a Pro victim's id>, share_id: <a folder id owned by that victim>, share_type: 1, number: <your own phone>}`. Then POST /api/share-folder-request-update with `{id: <the new request id>, status: 1}`. The victim's folder, its reminders and their attached files are copied into your account.
findings.impact: Enforces tenant isolation on the legacy sharing path by deriving the sharing identity from the authenticated session, preventing extraction of another customer's reminders, photographs and documents.
findings.refutation: Checked whether the added Pro-sender gate closes the hole — it does not; it is evaluated against the claimed sender, so it is satisfied by the victim's own subscription and if anything makes targeting easier to reason about. Checked whether the recipient gate blocks it — the recipient must be able to receive shares, which the attacker controls, and F4 grants that status to anyone. Checked whether acceptance re-validates the sender — `shareFolderRequestUpdate` correctly scopes the *receiver* to the session, which is exactly what lets the attacker accept their own forged request. Survives.
findings.remediation: Set `$senderId = (int) $this->user_id` and drop `sender_id` from the request contract, mirroring `ShareController::createInvite` line 69. Add the missing ownership check for `share_type = 2` against the `reminders` table. Then sweep the remaining legacy handlers for the same shape — several still accept a `user_id` the server already knows.

findings.title: Unrestricted file upload: the filename and target directory are attacker-controlled, and type validation is skipped entirely when `is_app=0`
findings.claim: `uploadFile()` stores the client's original filename verbatim into a directory named by the client's own `user_id` field, and for new reminders it is invoked outside the `$isApp` guard that decides whether any file-type or size rule is registered at all.

evidence.note: Directory from a request field, and the raw `mkdir` has no traversal guard — unlike `storeAs`, whose path Flysystem normalises. The audio path at line 1856 is identical.
No sanitisation, no extension allow-list, no server-generated name.
A request-controlled flag. The `File::types([...])` rules are registered only inside the `if ($isApp)` block that follows.
The new-reminder path calls the uploader outside that guard, so `is_app=0` writes the file with no type and no size validation.
Sibling comparison: the near-identical `uploadFileSync()` uses the authenticated id. The two copies have diverged and the `ReminderController` copy is the unsafe one (F27).

findings.reasoning: Three controls are missing on one path — the name, the directory and the type — and each is present elsewhere in the same codebase. Uploads land on the `public` disk, exposed through `public/storage` inside the document root (F12), so anything written is also served. Even where Flysystem normalises the path handed to `storeAs`, the bare `mkdir` above it is unguarded.
findings.reproduction: As any authenticated user, POST /api/reminder-create with `reminder_type=file`, `is_app=0`, `user_id=<another user's id>` and a multipart `reminder_value[]` file named `note.php`. No validator rule for `reminder_value` is registered, and the file is written under the named user's directory with the chosen name.
findings.impact: Closes the upload boundary by binding every stored file to the authenticated user's directory under a server-generated name with an enforced type and size, removing both the cross-tenant write and any possibility of a served executable.
findings.refutation: Checked whether `File::types()` would catch a disguised file on the validated path — it validates the content-guessed extension, so a valid JPEG carrying an appended payload passes while keeping a `.php` client filename; but the more direct issue is that `is_app=0` registers no rule at all. Checked whether Flysystem blocks traversal in the directory — it does for `storeAs`, but not for the preceding `mkdir` against `storage_path()`. Checked whether the storage quota constrains abuse — it applies but does not prevent the write. The remote-code-execution consequence is held as a caveat rather than asserted, because the host's PHP handler configuration was not observable.
findings.remediation: Derive the directory from `$this->user_id` only. Generate the stored filename server-side (`Str::uuid()` plus the validated extension) and keep the client's name in a separate display column. Move the `File::types()` rules outside the `$isApp` branch so every path is validated, and add the same rules to the sync uploader. Drop a `.htaccess` with `php_flag engine off` into `storage/app/public` as defence in depth.

findings.title: `GET /api/cron-reminders` is public: anyone can drive reminder dispatch, mutate recurrence state and read other users' reminder titles
findings.claim: The reminder-dispatch job is exposed as an unauthenticated GET route that writes to the `reminders` table and `echo`s each processed reminder's title into the response body ahead of the JSON payload.

evidence.note: Outside every auth middleware — no `auth.appUser`, no `jwt.verify`, no signed URL, no shared secret.
Every processed reminder's title — free-text user content — is written to whoever made the request.
The loop advances `reminder_send_on` and `reminder_send_on_last` on every recurring reminder it processes, so the endpoint mutates state as well as reading it.
A scheduler already exists and runs `general:notification` every minute, so the infrastructure to host this as a proper job is present and in use.

findings.reasoning: A scheduled job wearing an HTTP route as a costume — a common shared-hosting workaround that inherits none of a job's isolation. Because it writes as well as reads, repeated calls advance other users' recurring reminders; because the loop echoes before returning JSON, the response is both malformed and a disclosure channel for whatever is due that minute.
findings.reproduction: `curl https://api.eazyreminder.com/api/cron-reminders`. The body begins with the titles of every reminder due in that minute across all users, followed by the JSON envelope, and recurring reminders have their schedule pointer advanced.
findings.impact: Removes an unauthenticated write path into user data and stops the disclosure of other customers' reminder content, while making scheduled dispatch a first-class job with its own execution record.
findings.refutation: Checked whether `throttle:api` limits the damage — it caps one IP per minute, which prevents neither the disclosure nor the mutation. Checked whether the echoed output is discarded before the JSON response — Laravel prepends prior output to the response body rather than dropping it. Checked whether any network control restricts the route to a cron host — none exists in `.htaccess` or middleware. Survives.
findings.remediation: Move `CronController::index()` into an Artisan command and schedule it beside `general:notification` with `withoutOverlapping()`, then delete the route. If the host cannot run `schedule:run`, keep the route but require a long random secret compared with `hash_equals`. Delete the `echo` immediately either way — it is a one-line change that stops the disclosure on its own.

findings.title: The repository ships the front controller and rewrite rules that make the Laravel application root the web document root
findings.claim: `backend/index.php` and `backend/.htaccess` are committed and exist solely to let the project root be served as the document root; the rewrite serves any file that exists on disk before Laravel sees the request, and the only file protected is the one literally named `.env`.

evidence.note: A forwarding front controller at the project root. Tracked in git — it is a deliberate, shipped part of the deployment shape.
The only access control in the file. It matches the literal name `.env` and nothing else — not `.env.bak.*`, not `storage/`, not `composer.lock`.

Genuinely good, and verified: `.env`, `storage/firebase/` and `*firebase-adminsdk*.json` are all ignored, and a search of the working tree confirms no secret is committed. The exposure is created at deploy time, not in the repository.
The standard Laravel rules live here, in the directory that *should* be the document root — so the correct layout is already present and simply not the one used.

findings.reasoning: Laravel's security model rests on exactly one directory being web-reachable. This layout inverts that, and the single compensating rule covers one filename out of the many sensitive paths the framework's fixed structure makes guessable. A previously reviewed deployment of this backend confirmed the consequence: the Firebase service-account private keys, nine timestamped `.env` backups and a full source archive were all retrievable over HTTP from that host. The repository is clean; the shape it ships is what creates the exposure.
findings.reproduction: On the deployed host, request `/storage/firebase/<service-account>.json`, `/.env.bak.gmail` or `/composer.lock`. Each resolves to a file that exists, so the `!-f` rewrite condition fails and Apache serves it verbatim.
findings.impact: Eliminates the largest deployment exposure by ensuring no credential, log or source file can be retrieved over HTTP, and restores the standard Laravel boundary that every other control assumes.
findings.refutation: Checked whether the repository itself leaks anything, which would make this far worse — it does not; `.gitignore` is correct and no secret is tracked. Checked whether `Options -Indexes` mitigates it — that prevents directory listing, not direct retrieval of a known path. Checked whether the deployment might in fact point at `backend/public` — the forwarding `index.php` would be pointless if it did, and the deployed snapshot's error-log paths showed the project root in use. Survives.
findings.remediation: Point the hosting account's document root at `backend/public` and delete the root `index.php`; the correct `.htaccess` is already in `public/`. Where the plan forbids changing the document root, add explicit `<FilesMatch>` deny rules for `.env*`, `*.log`, `*.lock`, `*.zip`, `*.bak*` and everything under `storage/` as an interim measure. Either way, rotate the Firebase service-account keys, database password, SMTP password, JWT secret, RevenueCat webhook secret and Apple shared secret, all of which have been reachable.

findings.title: A hardcoded QA phone allowlist grants full paid entitlement in production, with no environment guard
findings.claim: Two phone numbers are hardcoded into an allowlist that grants Pro entitlement — sharing, share receipt and referral paid status — regardless of subscription state, environment or expiry, and the allowlist is consulted on the normal production code path.

evidence.note: Unconditional. There is no `app()->environment()` check, no feature flag and no expiry — the two numbers are always in the list.

The final return of `userCanSendShare()` — the entitlement predicate used by the share paths. Line 397 also returns it as the override when a paid subscription has *expired*, so a QA number keeps access after expiry.
`userHasActivePaid()` — the same bypass reaches referral entitlement.
An env-driven extension to the list. Under the cached config this reads empty, so it is inert in production — but the two built-in numbers above it are not.

findings.reasoning: A test affordance has been left on the production path. Its reach is entitlement rather than data — someone exploiting it obtains paid features they have not paid for, and keeps them after a real subscription would have lapsed. It matters beyond the lost revenue because paid status is a precondition elsewhere: F6's forged share requires a recipient who can receive shares, and this is one way to become one.
findings.reproduction: Complete Firebase phone verification for +91 9999999999 and register. `userCanSendShare` and `ReferralService::userHasActivePaid` both return true for that account with no subscription record. Whether the OTP is obtainable depends on the Firebase Console test-number configuration, which was not observable from the repository.
findings.impact: Restores paid features to paying customers only, and removes a permanent bypass that would survive any future change to the subscription logic.
findings.refutation: Checked whether the numbers are unreachable because no real user could hold them — Firebase Console test numbers are exactly the mechanism that makes them holdable, and the comment on line 331 says these are the built-in Firebase Console test mobiles. Checked whether the env-driven extension is the live risk — it is not; `env()` under the cached config returns empty, so only the two hardcoded numbers matter. Confidence is `Needs-runtime-check` because the Firebase test-number configuration is the deciding fact and it sits outside the repository. Priority set to P1 rather than P0 on that basis: the allowlist is certain, the ease of holding one of those numbers is not.
findings.remediation: Delete the built-in numbers and gate the whole helper on `app()->environment(['local','staging'])`, so a QA affordance cannot exist in production even when the env var is set. Confirm in the Firebase Console whether the two numbers are registered as test numbers and remove them if the project no longer needs them.
findings.rationale: De-escalated from P0 to P1 because reachability depends on an unverified Firebase Console setting rather than on the API alone. Kept in Phase 1 and gated as blocks-prod because the code itself is unambiguous and the fix is under a day.

findings.title: Session revocation was removed and nothing replaced it: a leaked token stays valid for 30 days
findings.claim: `JwtMiddleware` no longer compares the presented token against `users.session_token`, the comment records that the check was removed to stop multi-device logouts, and no blacklist or invalidate call exists anywhere — so with a 30-day TTL there is no way to retire a compromised token.

evidence.note: The removal, and the reason for it. The reason is legitimate — the old check was a single-column approximation of multi-device sessions — but no replacement was built.
43,200 minutes — 30 days. That is the full lifetime of a leaked token.
Logins still write `session_token` to the users table, so the column is maintained at some cost and read by nothing on the authorisation path.
The blacklist is enabled but nothing calls `JWTAuth::invalidate()` — a sweep of the controllers and middleware finds no logout or revocation path at all.

findings.reasoning: The system previously had a crude revocation mechanism and now has none. Every other finding that yields a token — F1, F2, and the QR handoff — therefore yields one that cannot be withdrawn for a month. The middleware does correctly reject tokens for deleted accounts, so the account-deletion path is covered; ordinary compromise is not.
findings.impact: Gives the team a way to end a session on demand, so a leaked or stolen token can be retired immediately instead of remaining valid for a month.
findings.refutation: Checked whether Passport or Sanctum provides revocation in parallel — both are installed but neither is wired into the API guard, which uses the `jwt` driver. Checked whether the removal was compensated elsewhere, for example by a shorter TTL — the TTL is 30 days, the longest value in the file. Downgraded from High to Medium because a valid token is still required; this is the absence of a control rather than a way through one.
findings.remediation: Model sessions properly rather than restoring the single-column check: add a `user_sessions` table keyed by device with a per-session identifier carried as a JWT claim, and have the middleware reject a token whose session row is missing or revoked. That gives per-device logout, a working 'sign out everywhere', and a kill switch for incident response. Shorten the TTL to hours with a refresh flow once revocation exists.

findings.title: A free user logging in from a new device has all their reminders and files silently deleted, outside any transaction
findings.claim: When a user with `is_paid = 0` logs in from a device whose `device_id` differs from the stored one, `login()` deletes their notifications, reminders and uploaded files before issuing the token — with no warning and after `DB::commit()`, so nothing can roll it back.

evidence.note: The trigger: a free user on a different device.

evidence.snippet:
// $response['message'] = 'Kindly log in using the device you utilized for the registration process.';
// return response()->json($response);
evidence.note: The original behaviour — refuse the login — is commented out immediately above the deletion that replaced it, unchanged since the previous review.
Followed by a loop that calls `fileDelete(...)` and `delete()` per reminder — files are unlinked from disk, not soft-deleted.

findings.reasoning: A device-binding policy was converted from 'refuse' to 'erase' without the data-loss consequence being reconsidered; the commented-out refusal directly above is the evidence. The ordering compounds it — the write happens after the transaction commits, so a mid-loop failure leaves a partially destroyed account with no rollback and no record of what was removed.
findings.reproduction: Register a free account and create reminders with photo attachments. Log in again with a different `device_id`. The login succeeds and every reminder, attachment and notification is gone.
findings.impact: Prevents silent, irreversible loss of a customer's reminders and photographs on an ordinary device change, and brings the remaining multi-step write inside a transaction.
findings.refutation: Checked whether the rows are soft-deleted and recoverable — `Reminder` uses a hard `delete()` and `fileDelete()` calls `unlink()`. Checked whether paid users are affected — they are not, confirming the intent was quota enforcement rather than a bug in the deletion itself. Priority set to P1 rather than P0 because the trigger is the account owner's own login rather than an attacker-controlled request.
findings.remediation: Restore the refusal, or replace the deletion with a device-transfer flow that states what will happen and requires confirmation. Whichever is chosen, move the write inside the transaction and record an audit row. As an immediate mitigation, comment out the deletion block and re-enable the message above it.
findings.rationale: High criticality (irreversible customer data loss) but not attacker-reachable, so P1 rather than P0. Kept in Phase 1 because it destroys customer data on every occurrence and the stop-gap is a one-line change.

findings.title: TLS certificate verification is disabled on all five outbound push calls, and the newest one was added this cycle
findings.claim: Every cURL call to Firebase Cloud Messaging sets `CURLOPT_SSL_VERIFYPEER = false`, so the project-wide OAuth access token is sent over connections whose certificate is not validated — and the pattern was copied into `FcmShareNotifier`, a service written during this development cycle.

evidence.note: The newest instance, in a service created for the share feature — the defect is still propagating into new code.
FCM v1 `messages:send`, carrying `Authorization: Bearer <google access token>`.
The legacy `fcm/send` path.
Fourth instance.
Fifth instance, in the scheduled general-notification command.

findings.reasoning: Disabling peer verification removes the only thing distinguishing Google's endpoint from an interceptor. The credential carried is not per-user but the project-wide FCM access token derived from the service account, so an interception yields the ability to push arbitrary notifications to every installed client. That a fifth copy appeared in new code shows this is being propagated by example rather than reasoned about each time.
findings.impact: Restores end-to-end transport security on the notification path, ensuring the Firebase access token and every payload reach only a verified Google endpoint.
findings.refutation: Checked whether these target an internal host where a private CA might justify the flag — all five target `fcm.googleapis.com`. Checked whether the host lacks a CA bundle, the usual reason this appears — `guzzlehttp/guzzle` and `google/apiclient` make verified calls from the same process to mint the token and succeed, so the bundle is present. Survives. Priority P1 rather than P0 because exploitation requires an on-path network position.
findings.remediation: Delete all five lines. Then replace the hand-rolled cURL with the `kreait/firebase-php` messaging client already in the dependency tree, which handles the token, transport and retries — that also removes the copy-by-example source.
findings.rationale: De-escalated from the P0 default for a High-criticality transport defect because exploitation needs an on-path position rather than an HTTP request.

findings.title: The Apple App Store shared secret is hardcoded in source
findings.claim: The App Store Connect shared secret used for receipt verification is written as a literal in `UserController`, in both the live method and a commented-out copy of it, and is therefore committed to the repository.

evidence.note: The shared secret as a literal in the `verifyReceipt` payload of the live method.
A second copy inside a commented-out earlier version of the same method — so removing one occurrence is not enough.

`.env` is correctly ignored and no environment file is committed, which is exactly why a literal in a controller is easy to miss: a reviewer checking for committed secrets finds a clean answer everywhere else.

findings.reasoning: Unlike the environment values, this credential is in version control and therefore in the history of every clone, including any held by former contributors. It also survives any rotation of `.env`, because nothing about the environment file references it.
findings.impact: Restores a single source of truth for credentials and makes rotation complete rather than partial, so a compromised secret can actually be retired.
findings.refutation: Checked whether the secret is inert because the surrounding verification logic is commented out (F21) — the method is still routed and still sends the value to Apple, and the constant remains a live shared secret for the production App Store account regardless of what the response is used for. Survives.
findings.remediation: Rotate the shared secret in App Store Connect, move it to `config/services.php` backed by an environment variable, and delete both occurrences including the commented block. Add secret scanning to the pipeline built in G1 so a literal of this shape fails the build.

findings.title: 50 of 81 catch blocks discard the exception, all of them in the older controllers
findings.claim: Counted per file, the API controllers contain 81 catch blocks of which 31 log the exception; the split is entirely by vintage — `ShareController` logs 9 of 9 and `TodoController` 8 of 9, while `ReminderController` logs 5 of 22 and `UserController` 1 of 8.

evidence.note: 22 catch blocks, 5 of which log. The rest return a generic apology and discard `$th`.
8 catch blocks, 1 logging — the worst ratio among the large controllers.
9 of 9 log. The pattern the rest should match, written by the same team this cycle.
The correct shape, in the newest large controller.
The exception to the vintage rule: 5 catch blocks, 0 logging, in a controller written this cycle — worth fixing before the habit re-establishes itself.

findings.reasoning: Catching `\Throwable` at the top of an action turns every defect into an identical apology with no trace, no error rate and no alert. The improvement in the new controllers is real and worth protecting; the legacy half is what still makes the security findings above operationally invisible, since probing those endpoints produces no signal at all.
findings.impact: Gives the team the ability to see, count and act on failures across the whole API rather than half of it, which is the precondition for verifying that any other fix worked.
findings.refutation: Verified by script rather than by eye, counting `catch (` occurrences against `Log::` within the following eight lines per file, after an initial grep-based estimate proved wrong. Checked whether Laravel's handler reports the swallowed ones anyway — it does not; an exception caught inside the action never reaches it. Survives, at a corrected count of 50 rather than the whole set.
findings.remediation: Add `Log::error($th->getMessage(), ['exception' => $th, 'route' => $request->path(), 'user_id' => $this->user_id])` to the 50 silent blocks, copying the shape already used in `ShareController`. Start with `WebLoginController`, which is new and should not have shipped without it. Then wire the error tracker from G3 so these reach a dashboard rather than a file.
findings.rationale: Escalated from P2 to P1 because the gap is systemic across the legacy half of the API and because it blocks verification of every other remediation in the roadmap.

findings.title: Reminder content, email addresses and IP addresses are written to the application log
findings.claim: The application logs whole sync payloads, user email addresses, phone numbers and caller IP addresses at INFO level, into a channel that does not rotate and — given the deployment layout in F12 — sits inside the document root.

evidence.note: Email addresses on every OTP send.
Both phone numbers written on every mismatch.
`[register-verify] existing-phone hit` logs the caller's IP address and user agent against a phone-number lookup.
The shipped template defaults to debug on the `stack` channel, which resolves to `single` — one file, no rotation. The deployed environment was observed using exactly this value.

findings.reasoning: Each line was added for a legitimate diagnostic reason, but together they make the log a secondary copy of the personal data the application holds, and F12 publishes the file. The `single` channel compounds it: nothing ages out, so the copy accumulates indefinitely.
findings.impact: Keeps personal data out of diagnostic output and off the public surface, reducing breach exposure and simplifying the retention obligations that apply to reminder content and contact details.
findings.refutation: Checked whether the `daily` channel's retention applies — `LOG_CHANNEL=stack` resolves to `single`, which has no retention. Checked whether the OTP code itself is exposed — that branch requires `MAIL_MAILER=log`, and the deployed value was `smtp`, so the code is not; the email address, phone number, IP and reminder content are. Survives.
findings.remediation: Replace identity fields in log context with opaque IDs — log `user_id`, not the email or phone — and remove the payload dumps. Set `LOG_LEVEL=warning` for production and switch the channel to `daily` so the file rotates. Fixing F12 removes the public exposure, but the content should not be there regardless.

findings.title: The six core legacy tables still carry no index or foreign key, while every table created this year has both
findings.claim: Of 67 migrations, 13 declare an index or foreign key and every one of them creates a table added in 2026; the original `reminders`, `folders`, `users`, `notifications`, `reminder_files` and `share_folder_requests` tables have nothing beyond their primary keys, and no later migration backfills them.

evidence.note: The new standard, and it is a good one — scoped uniqueness and indexed lookup columns.
The columns every reminder query filters on, and the ones the once-a-minute dispatch scans, with no index and no key.
The reverse migration names a table that does not exist — `reminder`, not `reminders` — so the rollback silently does nothing.

A sweep for `foreignId`, `constrained` and `->index(` across all 67 files returns 13, of which 5 are stock Laravel/Passport tables and 8 are the 2026 feature tables. No migration adds an index to a pre-2026 application table.

findings.reasoning: The practice changed without the existing schema being brought along, so the database is now two databases: a well-modelled recent half and an unconstrained legacy half that carries the highest-traffic tables. Referential integrity is enforced nowhere in that half, and the hand-written cascade logic differs between deletion paths, so orphaned rows are an ordinary outcome of any partial failure — which F11's untransacted deletion makes likely.
findings.impact: Guarantees a reminder always belongs to a real user and folder, removes the orphans partial deletions leave behind, and gives every user-scoped query an index instead of a table scan.
findings.refutation: Checked whether indexes might have been added directly on the production database outside the migration history — no live database was available, so the finding is stated on the migrations, which are the only reproducible definition of the schema; if undocumented indexes do exist they would be lost on any rebuild, which is the same problem. Checked whether the new tables' quality means the practice is now established — it is for new work, and the legacy backfill is what remains.
findings.remediation: Add one migration indexing `reminders.user_id`, `reminders.folder_id`, `reminders.reminder_send_on`, `reminders.reminder_datetime`, `folders.user_id`, `folders.parent_id`, `reminder_files.reminder_id`, `notifications.user_id` and both `share_folder_requests` participant columns — non-breaking, and it unlocks F24. Then clean up orphans and add foreign keys with explicit `onDelete` behaviour in a second migration. Fix the `dropIfExists('reminder')` typo while there.
findings.rationale: Escalated from P2 to P1 because it covers every high-traffic table in the system and because it caps the achievable outcome of F24 and F26 — the query work cannot pay off until the indexes exist.

findings.title: `ReminderController` is 2,518 lines and bypasses the service layer the rest of the codebase has started to adopt
findings.claim: One controller holds folder CRUD, reminder CRUD, contact lookup, legacy sharing, share acceptance, recurrence arithmetic, file upload, media deletion and cloud sync across 2,518 lines, while the newer features were built behind five service classes — so the codebase now has two architectures at once.

evidence.note: 2,518 lines. `createReminder` spans roughly lines 1045–1290; the recurrence arithmetic runs to several hundred more.
The counter-example: 167 lines, one responsibility, transactional, fully testable without HTTP. `AppPolicyService`, `ReferralService`, `EmailOtpService` and `FcmShareNotifier` follow the same shape.

Identity resolved in the constructor, which Laravel runs before route middleware — so `$this->user_id` is populated from a token `jwt.verify` has not yet validated, and is silently null on the unauthenticated routes in the same class.
The new sharing code validates the sender against the session; the legacy sharing code in ReminderController does not (F6). The split architecture is the reason the two disagree.

findings.reasoning: With no layer between HTTP and Eloquent in the legacy half, every action re-implements resolve-identity, validate, mutate and shape-response, and each re-implementation is a chance to get identity wrong. That is not speculative: F5, F6 and F7 are the same mistake made independently in three actions that would share one line in a service. The emerging service layer shows the destination is agreed; the legacy controller is what has not moved.
findings.impact: Makes the security fixes durable rather than local by giving identity resolution, authorisation and persistence a single home, and lets the newer and older halves of the codebase converge on one architecture.
findings.refutation: Checked whether the size is an artefact of generated code or large literals — it is hand-written branching logic. Checked whether the constructor's use of `authData()` is exploitable on its own — it is not, because `jwt.verify` still rejects an invalid token before the action runs; recorded here as fragility rather than as a separate finding.
findings.remediation: Extract in risk order: first an authorisation service or Laravel policies answering 'may this user touch this row', because F5, F6 and F7 all depend on it; then `FolderService`, `ReminderService` and `UploadService`, folding in the duplicated copies from F27; then the recurrence arithmetic into a unit-testable class. Move identity resolution out of the constructor into middleware-populated request attributes. Use `WebLoginService` as the template.
findings.rationale: Escalated from P2 to P1 because it blocks the durable form of the P0 authorisation fixes — without an authorisation layer, F5, F6 and F7 can only be patched site by site and the same class of defect will recur.

findings.title: Six thousand lines of new feature code shipped with no tests at all
findings.claim: `tests/` still contains only `Unit/ExampleTest.php` and `Feature/ExampleTest.php` — the files `laravel new` creates — despite the addition of QR web login, social sign-in, referrals, share groups and a to-do subsystem since the previous review.

evidence.note: The stock example asserting `/` returns 200. Unmodified.
The stock example asserting `true === true`. Unmodified.
Correctly configured and ready to run — the harness exists and has never been used.
`phpunit/phpunit`, `mockery/mockery` and `fakerphp/faker` are all installed as dev dependencies.

findings.reasoning: Every finding in this report must be fixed without a regression net, and several — F1, F2, F3, F5, F6, F7 — are precisely the kind of authorisation logic that is easy to fix in one place and reintroduce in another. The absence of tests is also why the divergences in F6, F15 and F27 persisted: nothing asserted that the two implementations of the same operation behave alike. Estimates throughout this report carry the 1.5x no-tests multiplier for this reason.
findings.impact: Establishes a regression net around the authentication, authorisation and sync paths so the Phase 1 security fixes stay fixed, and makes the architectural work in Phase 2 safe to attempt.
findings.refutation: Checked whether tests live elsewhere — a Postman collection sits in `mobile/` and in `Changes_and_Fixes/`, both manual and run by no pipeline. Checked whether the harness was abandoned rather than unused — `phpunit.xml` is intact and correctly configured. Survives.
findings.remediation: Do not chase coverage. Write one feature test per P0, asserting the specific invariant this review found violated: a login naming a different account than the credential proves is rejected; a token with no email claim cannot select an account by body email; a non-admin gets 403 from `/admin`; the webhook rejects a missing secret; `user-delete` refuses another user's ID; `share-folder` ignores a body `sender_id`; an upload cannot choose its directory or type. Each is a handful of lines, each fails today, and each pins one blocker. Then run them in the pipeline from G1.

findings.title: Laravel 9 is thirty months past end of security support and nothing scans the dependency tree
findings.claim: The application runs `laravel/framework` v9.52.21, whose security support ended in February 2024, on a PHP constraint of `^8.0.2` that permits an end-of-life PHP 8.0, and no automated vulnerability scanning exists anywhere in the repository.

evidence.note: `laravel/framework` v9.52.21 — unsupported for roughly thirty months as of this review. Unchanged since the previous assessment.
Permits PHP 8.0, itself end-of-life since November 2023. The runtime version on the host was not observable.

Three overlapping authentication packages remain installed — `laravel/passport`, `laravel/sanctum` and `php-open-source-saver/jwt-auth` — of which only jwt-auth is wired into `config/auth.php`, alongside two copies of the datatables package.

findings.reasoning: An unsupported framework means any vulnerability disclosed against Laravel 9 since early 2024 is permanent for this application, and nothing in the delivery process would surface one. The unused authentication packages widen the surface for no benefit — Passport in particular publishes routes and tables this application does not use.
findings.impact: Puts the platform back on a supported security-patch stream and makes its dependency set scannable, so a newly disclosed vulnerability can be found and fixed rather than discovered by an attacker.
findings.refutation: Checked whether a backported LTS or paid support arrangement covers Laravel 9 — Laravel publishes no such programme. Checked the wider tree for abandoned packages — `guzzlehttp/guzzle`, `symfony/*` 6.4 LTS, `league/flysystem` and `google/apiclient` are all current, so the framework itself is the exposure. Note that the previous review's claim that `composer.lock` was excluded from version control is **not** true of this repository: the lockfile is tracked, so builds are reproducible. The `.gitignore` entry that would have excluded it is stale and inert (F31). Priority de-escalated from P0 to P1 because remediation is a framework migration rather than a code fix.
findings.remediation: Plan the upgrade to Laravel 11 or 12 by way of 10, raise the PHP constraint to `^8.2`, and remove `laravel/passport`, `laravel/sanctum`, `laravel/ui` and the duplicate datatables package once their absence is verified in staging. Add `composer audit` to the pipeline as part of G5 so the next lapse is caught automatically.
findings.rationale: De-escalated from the P0 that High criticality plus public reachability would give, because the fix is a framework migration that must be sequenced after Phase 1 stabilisation rather than attempted alongside it.

findings.title: iOS receipt verification calls Apple and discards the answer, so App Store purchases are never validated
findings.claim: `receiptDataVerify()` posts the stored receipt to Apple's production endpoint, decodes the response, and then does nothing with it — every branch that acted on the status remains commented out, and the method returns nothing on the success path.

evidence.note: All handling — success, the 21007 sandbox-receipt fallback, and failure — is commented out. `$res` is assigned and never read.
The sandbox fallback branch, also commented out.
The route is live and inside the authenticated group, so it presents as a working control.

findings.reasoning: The endpoint has the shape of a purchase validation and none of the substance, which is worse than not having one: an operator reading the route list would reasonably conclude iOS purchases are verified. Combined with F4, where the webhook that actually grants entitlement is unauthenticated, and F9, where a hardcoded allowlist grants it outright, the entitlement system has no working verification on any path.
findings.impact: Restores a real verification decision on App Store purchases so entitlements follow Apple's answer rather than the request that asked for them.
findings.refutation: Checked whether the decision is made elsewhere and this endpoint is vestigial — `revenueCatWebhook` is the only other writer of `is_paid`, and F4 shows it is unauthenticated, so no working verification exists on either path. Checked whether it is dead code that could simply be deleted — it is routed and reachable, so it is live but inert. Survives.
findings.remediation: Either implement the decision — act on `status == 0`, retry against the sandbox endpoint on 21007, reject otherwise — or delete the endpoint and make a correctly authenticated RevenueCat webhook (F4) the single source of entitlement truth. Deleting is the smaller and more defensible change given RevenueCat is already integrated. Rotate the shared secret either way (F14).

findings.title: `die()` inside the reminder dispatch loop aborts the whole batch on the first failed push
findings.claim: `sendCustomNotification()` calls `die()` when cURL fails and is invoked from inside the per-reminder loop, so one transient network error to Google stops the entire minute's dispatch and every reminder after the failing one is neither sent nor recorded.

evidence.note: Terminates the PHP process mid-loop.
Called inside `foreach ($reminders as $value)`, before `saveNotification()` — so the in-app notification row for the remaining reminders is never written either.
Recurrence state for reminders processed earlier in the same loop has already advanced, so a re-run will not pick them up — the failure is not idempotent.

findings.reasoning: A single external failure becomes a total batch failure with no retry and no record. Because the loop advances the recurrence pointer before dispatch, reminders already processed are marked handled while those after the failure are lost outright. The product's core promise is that a reminder arrives; this is the path that breaks it, silently, and F15 ensures nobody finds out.
findings.impact: Ensures one failing push cannot stop every other customer's reminder from being delivered, and makes dispatch failures visible and retryable instead of silent and permanent.
findings.refutation: Checked whether an enclosing handler could salvage the batch — `die()` is not an exception and no handler runs. Checked whether the missed reminders are retried on the next minute's run — they are not, because the query selects on the current minute and the pointer has moved. Survives.
findings.remediation: Replace `die()` with a caught, logged failure that continues the loop, and record a per-reminder delivery outcome. Once F25 provides a queue, dispatch each reminder as its own job so a failure is isolated and retried automatically.
findings.rationale: Escalated from P2 to P1 because the loss is irreversible — a missed reminder is never re-attempted — and placed in Phase 1 because the fix is a one-line change with an outsized effect on the product's core function.

findings.title: Almost every API response returns HTTP 200 regardless of outcome, including authentication failures
