findings.claim: The controllers assemble a `status` field inside the JSON body and return HTTP 200 for it, so failures — including expired sessions and rejected authorisation — are indistinguishable from successes to any client, proxy or monitor reading the status line.

evidence.note: Authorisation failure returned as HTTP 200, with 404 as the in-body code and the word misspelt.
The convention declared per controller: 404 stands for 'validation failed' and 500 for 'an exception was caught', neither matching the HTTP meaning.
The counter-example: the newest endpoints do pass a real status code. The convention is being abandoned in new code, which makes a migration realistic.
Also returns real status codes. The split is again by vintage rather than by design.

findings.reasoning: The HTTP status line is the one part of a response that infrastructure understands without parsing. Collapsing it to 200 means error rates cannot be measured at the load balancer or in an APM tool, retry logic cannot distinguish failure from success, and the 401s that would reveal an attack in progress are invisible. The newer endpoints having moved on makes this a migration rather than a redesign.
findings.impact: Makes API failures visible to clients, proxies and monitoring by carrying the outcome in the HTTP status line, which is the precondition for meaningful error-rate alerting.
findings.refutation: Checked whether the mobile client depends on the 200 convention and would break — the client was not in scope, so this is treated as a migration constraint rather than dismissed, and the remediation proposes a versioned transition. Checked whether outer middleware rewrites the status — none does. Survives at P2 because nothing here is exploitable and the change touches a live client contract.
findings.remediation: Adopt the newer convention deliberately: return real status codes from a base controller helper, keep the in-body `status` field for one release so the existing client keeps working, migrate the client, then drop it. Standardise the error envelope centrally rather than assembling it by hand in every action.

findings.title: The once-a-minute dispatch query wraps every date column in `DATE_FORMAT()`, forcing a full scan of unindexed tables
findings.claim: Each of the seven `orWhere` clauses in the dispatch query compares `DATE_FORMAT(column, '%Y-%m-%d %H:%i')` against a string, which no index can serve, and the query runs every minute joined to `users` against a `reminders` table that has no secondary index at all.

evidence.note: The first of seven such predicates in the same query.
Joined to the full users table, with `reminders.user_id` unindexed (F17).
The whole result set is materialised into PHP memory with no chunking or limit.

findings.reasoning: Applying a function to the indexed side of a comparison makes the predicate non-sargable, so MySQL evaluates `DATE_FORMAT` for every row on each of seven branches, once a minute, indefinitely. The cost grows with the number of reminders ever created and the schedule is fixed, so it degrades on a timer rather than under load.
findings.impact: Cuts the standing database load of reminder dispatch to an indexed range scan, so delivery latency stays flat as the reminder table grows.
findings.refutation: Checked whether the interpolation into `DB::raw` is injectable — it is not; the format string is a literal and the compared value is bound. Checked whether a functional index could serve it — MySQL could with a generated column, but none exists. No runtime measurement was possible, so this is reasoned from query shape; the shape alone is decisive.
findings.remediation: Compare against a bounded range on the raw column — `whereBetween('reminder_datetime', [$minuteStart, $minuteEnd])` — which is sargable and semantically identical, then add the indexes from F17. Chunk the result rather than materialising it whole.

findings.title: No queue: uploads, mail and push delivery all run inline on the request thread
findings.claim: The shipped configuration sets `QUEUE_CONNECTION=sync`, there is no `app/Jobs` directory and no worker process, so every upload, FCM call and email is performed synchronously while the caller waits.

evidence.note: The `sync` driver runs jobs immediately in-process; dispatching to it is equivalent to calling the handler directly. The deployed environment was observed using the same value.
FCM delivery is a blocking cURL call inside the per-reminder loop — n sequential round trips to Google inside one HTTP request.
SMTP handshake and send on the request thread, so a slow mail host directly becomes a slow OTP endpoint.
The new share-notification service follows the same inline pattern, so the synchronous path is still being extended.

findings.reasoning: Every slow or failure-prone operation sits on the synchronous path, so the API's latency is the sum of its third parties' latencies and its error rate is theirs. It is also what makes F22 possible: a failure in an inline call can abort the request that triggered it.
findings.impact: Decouples response time from third-party latency and gives failed uploads, emails and notifications automatic retry, so a transient Google or SMTP outage no longer becomes a user-visible failure.
findings.refutation: Checked whether the shared hosting plan can run a persistent worker — this could not be determined without host access, which is why the remediation offers the `database` driver with a scheduled `queue:work --stop-when-empty` as the cPanel-compatible fallback. The finding stands either way: the configuration has no asynchrony of any kind.
findings.remediation: Switch to the `database` queue driver — the `failed_jobs` migration is already present — and move FCM delivery, mail and post-upload processing into jobs. Run a supervised worker where the host allows one, otherwise `queue:work --stop-when-empty` on the existing minute schedule.

findings.title: The sync endpoint issues per-row queries in nested loops and commits partial results with no transaction
findings.claim: For each reminder in a sync batch the handler runs a lookup, a write and a re-read, and for each attached file a further existence check and update, all inside nested loops with no enclosing transaction — so a failure part-way through leaves the account half-synced.

evidence.note: Query 1 per reminder, against unindexed `user_id` and `local_id` on the legacy table (F17).
A re-read of the row just written, to return its `updated_at` — a value the write already knew.
Inside the per-file loop, so a reminder with eight attachments re-reads the same row eight times.
File validation happens inside the loop, after earlier reminders in the batch have already been written — so a rejected file at position five leaves rows one to four committed and returns an error.

findings.reasoning: A batch endpoint written as a per-item loop inherits none of the properties a batch should have: it is O(n) in round trips and it is not atomic. The validation ordering makes the atomicity problem user-visible — a partially applied sync followed by an error is exactly the state the client's conflict resolution cannot reason about. The newer todo sync does better, but this legacy path still carries the reminder data.
findings.impact: Makes synchronisation atomic and bounded, so a batch either applies fully or not at all and a large sync completes in a handful of queries rather than several per row.
findings.refutation: Checked whether an outer transaction wraps the loop — `syncToCloud` opens none; the only `DB::beginTransaction` calls are inside helpers. Checked whether the re-read is necessary — it returns the server's authoritative `updated_at`, which the write already has, so it is avoidable. Survives.
findings.remediation: Validate the whole batch before writing anything, wrap the loop in one transaction, replace per-row lookups with a single `whereIn` on the batch's `local_id` values keyed into a map, and use the model instance already in hand instead of re-reading it.

findings.title: The sync and upload logic exists in three divergent copies, and one of the divergences is a security defect
findings.claim: `ReminderController::uploadFile`, `ReminderController::uploadFileSync` and `SyncController::uploadFileSync` are near-identical implementations of the same operation that have drifted apart — two derive the storage directory from the authenticated user and one from a request field.

evidence.note: Copy A: the request field. This is the copy carrying F7.
Copy B: the authenticated user. Same function, same purpose, correct.
Copy C — a third `uploadFileSync` inside ReminderController itself.
Both `reminder-media-sync` and `reminder-sync` are routed, so the duplicated sync entry points are all live.

findings.reasoning: This is the sibling comparison that made F7 identifiable: three implementations of one operation, two of them right, proving the third is a regression rather than house style. Duplication of this kind is normally a maintainability concern; here it has already produced a P0, and it means every future fix must be applied in three places or silently apply in one.
findings.impact: Removes the possibility of a fix landing in one copy and not the others by collapsing the sync and upload paths into a single implementation with one set of tests.
findings.refutation: Checked whether the copies serve genuinely different contracts — the request shapes differ slightly (`reminder_value.N` versus `reminder_value`), but the storage, validation and persistence semantics are identical and the differences are accidental. Survives.
findings.remediation: Collapse to one `UploadService` and one `SyncService` used by all routes, taking the safe behaviour from `SyncController` as the base, and delete the duplicates from `ReminderController`. Do this after F7 is patched, not instead of it.

findings.title: Eleven AdminApi controllers ship with no routes, carrying an unreachable second authentication implementation
findings.claim: `app/Http/Controllers/AdminApi/` contains eleven controllers, including a full password-based `AdminAuthController`, none of which is referenced by any route file in this repository — a comment records that the admin API was moved to a separate application.

evidence.snippet: // Admin API moved to frontend/admin-backend/ (separate Laravel app).
evidence.note: The explanation. The controllers were left behind when the routes went.
A correct password check — the only one in the codebase against a user credential — sitting in unreachable code while the live Blade panel has no role check at all (F3).
`admin.api` middleware is registered for these controllers and consequently applied to nothing.
Only `api.php`, `channels.php`, `console.php` and `web.php` exist; a search across all four for `AdminApi` returns nothing.

findings.reasoning: Roughly a thousand lines of security-relevant code sit in the repository in a state where nobody can tell whether they are live. That ambiguity is the cost: a reader auditing admin authentication finds a competent implementation and may reasonably conclude the admin surface is well protected, when the surface that is actually reachable is the Blade panel with no role check.
findings.impact: Removes ambiguity about which admin surface is live and which code is security-relevant, so future review effort lands on the code that actually serves requests.
findings.refutation: Checked whether the routes are registered dynamically by a service provider rather than a route file — `RouteServiceProvider` loads only `api.php` and `web.php`. Checked whether the separate admin application lives in this repository and might load them — `frontend/admin-backend/` is not present in this repo. Confirmed unreachable.
findings.remediation: Delete the `AdminApi` directory and the `admin.api` registration if the separate admin application owns that code now, or restore its routes if it does not. Either way settle F3 first, since the Blade panel is what is currently exposed.

findings.title: Three endpoints answer for records the caller does not own, two of them without authentication
findings.claim: `check-reminder-available` confirms whether any reminder ID exists with no authentication, `checkTrialExpiry` reports the trial state of any user ID in the request body, and `insert-subscription` is an unauthenticated backfill that iterates every user on each call.

evidence.note: Outside every authentication middleware; the handler queries by `reminder_id` with no user scoping.
`$this->user_id` is resolved in the constructor and not used; the body's `user_id` selects the row.
A one-off data backfill exposed as a public GET; each call inserts a history row per paid user, so repeated calls duplicate rows without bound.

findings.reasoning: None of the three discloses content — an existence bit, a boolean trial flag, and a write that only duplicates existing data — which is why they are Low rather than joining F5 and F6. They are grouped because they share one root cause with those findings: the identifier comes from the request instead of the session and nobody checks who is asking.
findings.impact: Closes the remaining unauthenticated read and write paths so every endpoint answers only for the caller's own records, completing the tenant-isolation work begun in Phase 1.
findings.refutation: Checked whether `check-reminder-available` returns reminder content — it returns only an `is_available` flag, so it is an existence oracle rather than a disclosure. Checked whether `insert-subscription` can corrupt entitlement — it writes only to `subscription_histories`, which feeds the history list shown at login, so the impact is duplicate rows rather than false entitlement. Downgraded from Medium on that basis.
findings.remediation: Scope `checkTrialExpiry` to `$this->user_id`, move `check-reminder-available` behind `jwt.verify` and scope it to the caller, and delete `insert-subscription` — run it as an Artisan command if the backfill is still needed.

findings.title: The `auth.appUser` middleware is a static header check named as authentication, and emits a contradictory CORS header pair
findings.claim: The middleware registered as `auth.appUser` performs no authentication — it checks for one of three hardcoded `os_key` header values — and on success stamps `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` together with `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`, a pair no browser accepts, overriding the project's CORS configuration.

evidence.note: Three hardcoded constants any caller can send. A client-type tag, not a credential.
Browsers reject a wildcard origin combined with credentials, so the pair is inert — but it overrides what `HandleCors` computed from `config/cors.php`.

The name is the problem: a reader of `routes/api.php` sees `auth.appUser` wrapping the entire route file and reasonably concludes those routes are authenticated — which is how the genuinely unauthenticated ones below it stay unnoticed.

findings.reasoning: The header check is a reasonable way to filter casual traffic and claims to be no more than that anywhere except in its own name — but the name is what a reader of the route file sees. The CORS headers are inert in browsers, so this is hygiene rather than exposure.
findings.impact: Removes a misleading security signal from the route definitions and leaves one coherent CORS policy in configuration, so the real authentication boundary is legible to the next reader.
findings.refutation: Considered reporting the CORS pair as a genuine cross-origin exposure — refuted, because the specification requires browsers to reject a wildcard origin alongside credentials, and the API is token-authenticated rather than cookie-authenticated, so there is no ambient credential to steal. Considered reporting the header check as an authentication bypass — refuted, because it does not claim to authenticate a user and every route needing identity is additionally behind `jwt.verify` or `verify.firebase`. Downgraded to a Low naming and configuration issue.
findings.remediation: Rename the middleware to `client.type` so the route file stops implying authentication. Delete the four manual CORS headers and let `HandleCors` apply `config/cors.php`. Fix the status code and the misspelt message while there.

findings.title: Repository hygiene: a stale `.gitignore` entry for a tracked lockfile, and a snapshot directory checked in beside the code
findings.claim: `.gitignore` lists `composer.lock`, which is nonetheless tracked — so the file is committed today only because it predates the rule, and a `Changes_and_Fixes/` directory of loose controller and migration copies sits beside the live application.

evidence.note: Inert while the file stays tracked — `.gitignore` does not affect tracked files — but it would silently stop the lockfile being committed if it were ever removed and re-added, which is exactly how reproducible builds get lost.
Confirmed tracked via `git ls-files`. Builds are reproducible today; the rule above says they should not be.
Loose copies of controllers, models, migrations and a Postman collection checked in beside the live application, with no indication of which revision they correspond to.

findings.reasoning: Neither item causes harm today. Both make it ambiguous which file is authoritative, and the `.gitignore` line in particular is a trap that fires quietly at the worst moment — the lockfile is the only thing making the dependency set in F20 reproducible.
findings.impact: Removes ambiguity about which files are authoritative and protects the reproducibility of the dependency set that the framework upgrade will depend on.
findings.refutation: Checked whether the previous review's stronger claim — that the lockfile was excluded from version control — holds for this repository: it does not. `git ls-files` confirms the file is tracked, so that finding is corrected here rather than repeated. Only the stale rule remains.
findings.remediation: Delete the `composer.lock` line from `.gitignore`. Move `Changes_and_Fixes/` out of the application directory or delete it, relying on git history for the same information.

gaps.why: There is no CI configuration anywhere in the repository — no `.gitlab-ci.yml`, no `.github/workflows`, no `Jenkinsfile` — despite an active GitLab remote and a branch-per-feature workflow visible in the history. Nothing runs on a change: not the tests F19 will add, not a linter, not a secret scan. Every fix in this roadmap would be verified only by whoever wrote it.
gaps.recommendation: Add a GitLab CI pipeline with three stages: `composer install --no-dev`, `php artisan test`, and a secret scan. Gate merges into the working branch on it. Add a deploy stage that ships an artefact and runs `migrate --force` and `config:cache`, so the deployment steps stop being typed into a shell by hand.

gaps.why: No error tracker is configured — no Sentry, Bugsnag or Flare DSN in `.env.example` or `config/`, and `app/Exceptions/Handler.php` is the stock stub. Combined with the 50 silent catch blocks in F15, failures are invisible until a user reports them, which is why none of the defects in this report were noticed in production.
gaps.recommendation: Wire Sentry into `Handler::register()`, set a release identifier per deploy, and alert on error rate and on any 5xx from the authentication, webhook and dispatch routes. Do this in Phase 1 so the Phase 1 fixes can be verified in production rather than assumed.

gaps.why: No backup configuration, schedule or restore procedure appears anywhere in the repository, and the previously reviewed host carried only two ad-hoc source archives — code, not data. The application holds the only copy of every user's reminders, to-do boards and uploaded photographs, and F11 deletes some of them on an ordinary device change.
gaps.recommendation: Schedule a nightly `mysqldump` plus a copy of `storage/app/public` to storage outside the hosting account, retain 30 days, and rehearse a restore into a scratch database once before the next release and quarterly thereafter. Record the measured restore time as the recovery objective.

gaps.why: Nothing checks the dependency tree for known vulnerabilities, which is how a framework thirty months past end of security support (F20) stayed in place unremarked across a major feature cycle. Nothing scans for committed credentials either, which is how the Apple shared secret in F14 survived in source.
gaps.recommendation: Add `composer audit` and a secret scanner as blocking stages in the pipeline from G1, and subscribe the repository to automated dependency update proposals.

gaps.why: One environment exists. There is a single environment template, and the development escape hatch in `VerifyFirebaseIdToken` is guarded only by `config('app.env') === 'local'`, so there is nowhere to verify a change before customers see it. Every fix in this roadmap would otherwise be tested in production, including the authentication changes.
gaps.recommendation: Stand up a staging environment with its own database, Firebase project and RevenueCat sandbox, deployed by the same pipeline as production, and make it the gate the pipeline promotes through.

gaps.why: The hosting account is configured by hand. The `docker/` directory is Laravel Sail's local scaffolding and describes nothing about the production host — PHP version, extensions, cron entries, document root and TLS exist only as settings someone once clicked. That is also what allows the document-root layout in F12 to persist unnoticed.
gaps.recommendation: Capture the runtime as a Dockerfile plus a platform manifest, including the corrected document root from F12 and the cron entry that drives dispatch, and move to a host that can run it. This is the natural point at which to leave shared cPanel hosting.

gaps.why: There is no request ID, metric or trace anywhere. Because most responses are HTTP 200 (F23), even the platform's own access logs cannot separate failure from success, so no layer — application, platform or database — carries a signal that would show a degradation or an attack in progress.
gaps.recommendation: Add a correlation-ID middleware stamping every request and log line, then emit counters and latency histograms for the authentication, sync and dispatch paths. Sequence after F23, since error-rate metrics are meaningless while every response is 200.

gaps.capability: Data retention and PII handling policy
gaps.why: Nothing ages out. The `single` log channel never rotates and holds reminder content and IP addresses (F16); notifications, subscription histories, share requests and the new todo activity tables all grow without bound, with `insert-subscription` (F29) able to inflate one on demand; and deleted users are sometimes soft-deleted and sometimes hard-deleted with no stated rule. For a system holding phone numbers, email addresses, collaborator relationships and personal photographs, the retention position is undefined.
gaps.recommendation: Define and implement retention: rotate logs daily with a 14-day window, prune notifications and todo activity beyond 90 days, settle on one deletion semantic for users and apply it consistently, and document what personal data is held, where, and for how long.

refutedCandidates.claim: `POST /api/app-config` is an unauthenticated configuration write, since it sits behind only the static `os_key` header check.
refutedCandidates.reasoning: A compensating control exists and is correct: `AppConfigController::update` requires an `X-App-Policy-Admin-Key` header compared with `hash_equals` against `config('app_policy.admin_key')`, and returns 403 when the configured key is empty. It fails closed, reads from config rather than `env()` so it survives `config:cache`, and compares in constant time. This is the correct pattern, and it is cited in F4 as the sibling the RevenueCat webhook should match.

refutedCandidates.claim: The QR web-login flow lets an attacker who guesses or races a login token capture another user's session.
refutedCandidates.reasoning: Traced the whole flow. Tokens are 48 random characters (~248 bits after the lowercasing), expire in five minutes, and both `confirm` and `poll` run inside `DB::transaction` with `lockForUpdate`, so the confirm/consume race is closed. The JWT is handed over exactly once and `session_token` is nulled on consumption; a session already confirmed by a different user is rejected. This is the best-built authentication code in the repository and is recorded under positive posture instead.

refutedCandidates.claim: SQL injection through the raw-SQL sites across the controllers.
refutedCandidates.reasoning: Traced every operand. The `orderByRaw("FIELD(file_extension, ...)")` sites interpolate a literal extensions array declared a few lines above; the `DATE_FORMAT` sites interpolate only column names, with the compared value bound as a parameter by the query builder; the remaining `orderByRaw` calls are static `CASE WHEN` expressions. No request-derived value reaches any raw fragment. The performance consequence of the `DATE_FORMAT` predicates survives separately as F24.

refutedCandidates.claim: `env('QA_PRO_PHONES')` lets anyone with environment access silently grant Pro entitlement to arbitrary phone numbers in production.
refutedCandidates.reasoning: The variable is read with `env()` outside a config file, so under the cached configuration the deployment uses it resolves to an empty string and the env-driven extension is inert — the same mechanism that breaks the webhook guard in F4 happens to disable this. What is not inert is the pair of phone numbers hardcoded directly above it, which need no environment variable at all. Reported at that reduced scope as F9.

refutedCandidates.claim: `TodoController` exposes other users' boards through the shared-board merge in `syncGet`.
refutedCandidates.reasoning: `syncGet` opens by rejecting a request with no session user, derives `$uid` from the session, and builds the shared set from `sharedBoardScopes($uid)` — a server-side lookup of collaborations that name this user. The owner id passed to `todoGraphForOwnerBoard` comes from that lookup, never from the request. Every action in the controller follows the same shape.

refutedCandidates.claim: `ShareController` repeats the `sender_id` trust defect found in the legacy sharing code.
refutedCandidates.reasoning: It accepts the same field and validates it: `if ($senderId !== (int) $this->user_id)` rejects the request before any work is done. Group and membership operations are likewise scoped with `->where('owner_id', (int) $this->user_id)`. The new sharing subsystem is correct; it is the legacy `ReminderController::shareFolder` that is not, which is what establishes F6 as a gap rather than a house convention.

refutedCandidates.claim: The `api` rate limiter is ineffective because it keys on `$request->user()?->id`, which is null for JWT-authenticated requests.
refutedCandidates.reasoning: The expression falls back to `$request->ip()` when the user is null, so a limit always applies. The `auth` limiter additionally enforces two independent buckets — per-phone and per-IP — and Laravel ANDs an array of limits. A third named limiter, `throttle:web-login`, was added for the QR endpoints. Rate limiting remains one of the better-constructed parts of this codebase.

refutedCandidates.claim: The email OTP can be brute-forced, since `EmailOtpService::verify()` re-extends the cache TTL on every failed attempt.
refutedCandidates.reasoning: The TTL extension is real, but the attempt counter is incremented in the same write and the code is discarded at five failures, so the longer window cannot be used. A six-digit code with five attempts gives a 1-in-200,000 chance per issued code, and the `auth` limiter caps request rate per IP. Adequately defended.

refutedCandidates.claim: Mass assignment through `User::$fillable`, which omits `is_admin`, `is_paid` and `subscription_details` while the table carries them.
refutedCandidates.reasoning: The narrow `$fillable` is the safe direction — it excludes the privileged columns from mass assignment. Every write to `is_admin`, `is_paid` or `subscription_details` is an explicit property assignment on a model instance, not a `create()` or `fill()` from request data. The one place that sets `is_paid` from a request body is the webhook, which is F4 — an authentication defect, not a mass-assignment one.

refutedCandidates.claim: `FIREBASE_VERIFY_SKIP_LOCAL` allows the Firebase token check to be disabled in production by setting an environment variable.
refutedCandidates.reasoning: The escape hatch is guarded by `config('app.env') === 'local'` evaluated first, and the deployed environment reports `production`. The variable alone cannot enable it, and under the cached config it reads as null in any case. The middleware's real weakness is the relaxed phone-claim branch, reported as part of F1.

refutedCandidates.claim: Controllers resolving `authData()` in their constructor authenticate before the middleware runs, letting an unvalidated token populate `$this->user_id`.
refutedCandidates.reasoning: Laravel does run controller constructors before route middleware, so `$this->user_id` is indeed set from a token `jwt.verify` has not yet checked. But the action never executes unless the middleware subsequently passes, so no unvalidated identity reaches a response. Real fragility, no exploitable consequence — folded into F18 rather than reported separately. Note that `TodoController` and `ShareController` additionally assert `empty($this->user_id)` inside each action, which is the belt-and-braces form.

refutedCandidates.claim: `composer.lock` is excluded from version control, so the dependency set is not reproducible.
refutedCandidates.reasoning: This was reported against an earlier deployed snapshot and does not hold for the repository. `git ls-files` confirms `backend/composer.lock` is tracked; the `.gitignore` entry naming it is stale and inert, because `.gitignore` does not affect already-tracked files. The correction is recorded, and the residual trap is reported at Low severity as F31.

positivePosture.title: The QR web-login flow is the best-built authentication code in the repository
positivePosture.detail: `WebLoginService` issues a 48-character random token with a five-minute TTL, performs both confirmation and consumption inside `DB::transaction` with `lockForUpdate` so the confirm/consume race is closed, hands the JWT over exactly once and nulls it on consumption, rejects a session already confirmed by a different account, and distinguishes pending, expired and consumed states explicitly. It was written this cycle and shows the standard the team is capable of.

positivePosture.title: The newest administrative endpoint gets the secret comparison exactly right
positivePosture.detail: `AppConfigController::update` reads its key from `config()` rather than `env()` so it survives `config:cache`, returns 403 when the configured key is empty rather than skipping the check, and compares with `hash_equals`. All three properties are the ones the RevenueCat webhook lacks (F4), which means the remediation there is to copy a pattern the team has already written rather than to introduce one.

positivePosture.title: The new share and to-do subsystems enforce identity correctly
positivePosture.detail: `ShareController::createInvite` rejects a request whose body `sender_id` does not match the session, and its group and membership operations scope every query with `->where('owner_id', $this->user_id)`. `TodoController` opens each of its actions by rejecting a missing session user and derives shared-board access from a server-side collaboration lookup rather than from the request. Roughly 2,100 lines of new authorisation-sensitive code, with no cross-tenant defect found in it.

positivePosture.title: Every table created this year is properly indexed and scoped
positivePosture.detail: The eight 2026 migrations — share invites, share groups, todo boards, lists, cards, collaborators, activities, referrals and web-login sessions — consistently index their lookup columns and declare `unique(['user_id','local_id'])` where the sync model requires it. The schema practice has demonstrably changed; what remains is backfilling the legacy tables (F17).

positivePosture.title: Error logging has become the norm in new code
positivePosture.detail: `ShareController` logs the exception in 9 of 9 catch blocks and `TodoController` in 8 of 9, against 5 of 22 in `ReminderController`. The habit is establishing itself in exactly the places being actively developed, which makes the remaining backfill (F15) a mechanical exercise rather than a change of culture.

positivePosture.title: A service layer has begun to emerge, and its members are well formed
positivePosture.detail: `WebLoginService`, `AppPolicyService`, `ReferralService`, `EmailOtpService` and `FcmShareNotifier` each carry a single responsibility, are constructor-injected where used, and are testable without HTTP. `EmailOtpService` remains exemplary: the OTP is hashed rather than stored, generated with `random_int`, capped at five attempts, and discarded on success.

positivePosture.title: The repository itself is clean of secrets
positivePosture.detail: Verified rather than assumed: `.gitignore` excludes `.env`, `storage/firebase/` and `*firebase-adminsdk*.json`, and a search of the working tree confirms no environment file or service-account key is tracked. `composer.lock` is committed, so the dependency set is reproducible. The credential exposure in F12 is created by the deployment layout, not by the repository.

positivePosture.title: Rate limiting is deliberate and has been extended with the new surface
positivePosture.detail: The `auth` limiter enforces two independent buckets — 5/min per phone and 30/min per IP — returned as an array so Laravel applies both, with a comment explaining why the per-IP bucket is needed against enumeration. A third limiter, `throttle:web-login`, was added alongside the QR endpoints rather than leaving them on the global default.

phases.name: Stabilisation & Risk Mitigation
phases.objective: Close every production blocker and stop the ongoing data loss. All nine P0 findings sit here, along with the five Phase-1 P1 items and the three missing capabilities that make the rest of the work verifiable — a pipeline, error tracking and a real backup. Most items are a day or less, because in almost every case the correct implementation already exists elsewhere in the repository and only needs applying.

phases.name: Architecture & Scalability
phases.objective: Make the Phase 1 fixes permanent and let the two halves of the codebase converge. An authorisation layer so the tenant-isolation fixes cannot regress, a test suite that pins them, error logging backfilled across the legacy controllers, indexes on the legacy tables, a supported framework, and the queue the synchronous paths need.

phases.name: Optimisation & Governance
phases.objective: Contract, hygiene and operational maturity — finish the migration to real HTTP status codes, collapse the duplicated sync and upload code, remove the unrouted admin controllers, and put retention, infrastructure-as-code and correlated telemetry in place.

architecturalRecommendations.current: Six endpoints still accept `user_id`, `sender_id` or `{id}` from the request and use it to scope or authorise, while the newer controllers derive identity from the session.
architecturalRecommendations.recommended: Identity is derived from the authenticated session in one place, and no handler reads a caller identifier from the request.
architecturalRecommendations.recommendation: Extract the check `ShareController` already performs into an authorisation service or Laravel policies, apply it to the legacy handlers, and delete the caller-identifier fields from those request contracts. This single change removes the root cause of F5, F6, F7 and F29.

architecturalRecommendations.current: Proof of identity and selection of the account come from different places on two paths, and the middleware skips its cross-check whenever a field is absent.
architecturalRecommendations.recommended: Each route declares the proof it requires, and the account acted on is always the one the proof names.
architecturalRecommendations.recommendation: Make `VerifyFirebaseIdToken` assert positively per route rather than skipping when the body omits a phone, and resolve accounts only from verified claims — the fixes for F1 and F2 are the same fix seen twice.

architecturalRecommendations.current: One webhook reads its secret with `env()` and skips the check when empty; another endpoint reads `config()`, fails closed and compares in constant time.
architecturalRecommendations.recommended: Every shared secret is read from config, checked fail-closed, and compared with `hash_equals`.
architecturalRecommendations.recommendation: Make `revenueCatWebhook` structurally identical to `AppConfigController::update`, then grep for `env(` outside `config/` as a standing rule.

architecturalRecommendations.current: Two architectures coexist: five well-formed services behind the new features, and a 2,518-line controller talking straight to Eloquent behind the old ones.
architecturalRecommendations.recommended: Controller → service → repository throughout, with domain logic testable without HTTP.
architecturalRecommendations.recommendation: Extract in risk order — authorisation first, then folder, reminder and upload services, folding in the duplicated copies from F27. Use `WebLoginService` as the template; it is already the right shape.

architecturalRecommendations.current: Reminder dispatch is a public unauthenticated GET that mutates state, echoes user content, calls FCM inline and `die()`s on the first failure.
architecturalRecommendations.recommended: Dispatch is an Artisan command on the scheduler, with each delivery a queued, retryable job.
architecturalRecommendations.recommendation: Move `CronController::index` into a command scheduled `withoutOverlapping()`, delete the route and the `echo`, and dispatch per-reminder jobs once the queue from F25 exists.

architecturalRecommendations.current: Most responses are HTTP 200 with the outcome in the body, and 50 of 81 catch blocks discard the exception — but the newest endpoints do neither.
architecturalRecommendations.recommended: HTTP status carries the outcome, one error envelope is produced centrally, and every caught exception is recorded.
architecturalRecommendations.recommendation: Backfill `Log::error` across the legacy catch blocks first — mechanical, and it unblocks verification of everything else — then migrate status codes behind an API version so the mobile client can follow the newer endpoints.

architecturalRecommendations.current: The 2026 tables are indexed and keyed; the six core legacy tables have neither, and cascade behaviour is hand-written and inconsistent between deletion paths.
architecturalRecommendations.recommended: Relationships modelled as foreign keys with explicit delete behaviour, and every filtered column indexed.
architecturalRecommendations.recommendation: Ship indexes on the legacy tables first — non-breaking, and it unlocks F24 — then clean up orphans and add constraints in a second migration.

architecturalRecommendations.current: No CI, no staging, no IaC; deployment is manual and the deployment shape itself is a security finding.
architecturalRecommendations.recommended: Every change tested and deployed by a pipeline, through staging, from a reproducible artefact.
architecturalRecommendations.recommendation: Pipeline and error tracking in Phase 1, staging and dependency scanning in Phase 2, and treat the move off shared cPanel hosting in Phase 3 as the point at which infrastructure-as-code becomes possible.

capabilities.practice: Service layer and testable domain logic
capabilities.notes: Five well-formed services behind the new features; the legacy half still runs from a 2,518-line controller (F18).

architecturalNarrative:
This codebase is in the middle of a transition, and almost every finding in this report is a consequence of being caught halfway. The newer half — QR web login, share invites and groups, the to-do subsystem, referrals, app config — is built the way it should be: behind services, deriving identity from the session, checking ownership before acting, indexing its tables, logging its exceptions, returning real HTTP status codes, and guarding its one administrative endpoint with a fail-closed constant-time comparison. The older half still runs from a 2,518-line controller that talks directly to Eloquent, reads caller identity out of the request body, swallows its exceptions and returns 200 for everything. The two halves disagree, and where they disagree the older one is wrong.

That pattern is what makes the report unusually actionable. Sibling comparison did most of the work here: `ShareController` validates the same `sender_id` field that `ReminderController::shareFolder` trusts blindly; `AppConfigController` reads its secret from config and fails closed where `revenueCatWebhook` reads `env()` and fails open; `EnsureAdminApiUser` performs precisely the `is_admin` check the live Blade panel lacks; `SyncController::uploadFileSync` scopes the storage directory to the session user where its twin in `ReminderController` takes it from the request. In each pair the correct implementation was written by the same team, usually more recently. The remediation is propagation, not design.

The exception — and the reason this is a blocking report rather than a maintenance one — is the authentication boundary, which has moved backwards. Proof of identity and selection of the account have always come from different fields on the `/login` password branch, but the middleware used to demand a phone number in the body and cross-check it against the token, which constrained the damage. Accommodating social login relaxed that check to 'skip when the body has no phone', and in doing so removed the constraint from the older defect and created a second one in the new `socialLogin` handler, where an unverified body email can select an account and permanently bind the caller's Firebase UID to it. Two paths, one structural error, both reachable with a free account.

Underneath all of it, the delivery position has not moved at all. There is still no pipeline, no staging environment, no error tracking, no infrastructure definition and no evidence of a tested backup, and the deployment still serves the Laravel application root to the internet. Roughly 6,000 lines of new feature code shipped in this cycle with two stock example tests to cover them. The engineering quality visible in the new code is real; what is missing is anything that would catch the code that does not meet that standard — which is precisely how a relaxed middleware check and a hardcoded QA allowlist reached production without comment.
lookingAhead:
The nine blockers are cheaper to close than their severity suggests, because for eight of them the correct implementation already exists somewhere in this repository. Applying `admin.api` to the Blade group is one line. Making the RevenueCat webhook match `AppConfigController` is four. Setting `$senderId = $this->user_id` in `shareFolder` mirrors `ShareController` line 69. Deleting the `echo` from the dispatch loop is one line and stops a live disclosure on its own. Phase 1 is thirty-five days including a pipeline, error tracking and a real backup, and none of it requires structural change.

Two things should happen before any of that. Rotate every credential that has been reachable from the document root — correcting the layout stops future retrieval, not past retrieval, and there is no way to know from here whether anyone has looked. And confirm the three runtime facts this review could not observe: whether PHP executes from the storage directory, whether the two hardcoded QA phone numbers are still registered as Firebase test numbers, and whether the host takes and tests database backups. Each is minutes of work and each affects the ordering of the first week.

Beyond Phase 1 the goal is convergence. The authorisation service in Phase 2 is what stops the tenant-isolation fixes from regressing the next time someone adds a handler; the tests are what make that verifiable; the legacy indexes and the framework upgrade remove the two constraints that cap everything else. The direction of travel in this codebase is already correct — the newer code is markedly better than the older code, and the team has fixed several past defects properly and documented why. What is missing is the mechanism that would make that improvement uniform rather than incidental, and that is what the roadmap is mostly buying.
